newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia debt futures dip as rates left unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Australia debt futures dip as rates left unchanged.

text.p: *Australian debt futures briefly dipped after the RBA left policy unchanged, although speculation of a further easing is likely to persist after the recent run of weak data.

Australian debt futures briefly dipped after the Reserve Bank left policy unchanged, although speculation of a further easing is likely to persist after the recent run of weak data, particularly on the labour force.

September bill futures dipped to 94.88 after touching 94.92 prior to the RBA's usual announcement time at 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT), but still equated to a cash rate of 5.12 compared with official 5.5 percent official rates.
"We do see the potential for a further rate cut, but we would expect the Reserve Bank board to meet first," said Craig James, senior economist at Colonial State Bank.
"We would see it being extremely likely that you would get a rate cut something like July 3, after the Reserve Bank board meets and the FOMC keeps policy unchanged," said James.

Concerns that the Federal Reserve could tighten policy, possibly preventing a local easing, lessened somewhat after U.S. retail sales on Thursday fell for the third consecutive month in May, a run not seen since September/November 1981.

Thursday's local data showing an unexpected slump of over 40,000 in employment and a rise to 8.8 percent in unemployment in May sparked a fierce rally in the debt market, taking the 10-year bond yield close to 7.0 percent.
The RBA board meets on July 1 and the FOMC meets on July 1/2.

The only shining light in the economy at the moment appears to be the housing sector. Retail trade recorded back-to-back monthly falls in March/April, expectations for capital expenditure for 1997/98 have weakened and inflation remains benign. The May employment fall was the largest monthly fall since 1993 while recent business and consumer surveys have also been glum despite recent rate cuts.
In the absence of a rate cut, the bond market will now concentrate on the roll over to September from June futures contracts ahead of Monday's expiries.

The market showed a widening bias against the dollar bloc after Thursday's sharp narrowing, particularly at the short end after rates were left on hold. Canadian debt was strong on waning fears of a Fed tightening and the 30-year spread to the U.S. went to a negative for the first time.
